column5: revelation retained, then taught
column6: The commentary moves from the reciter who is not made to forget to a command to remind others; Deuteronomy tells eyewitnesses not to let what they saw leave their heart and to make it known to children.

column5: hearing, fear, teaching children
column6: At Horeb the gathered people hear God's words in order to learn fear and teach their children, closely joining the commentary's recipient who fears with its outward act of reminding.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B006); Hebrew זכרון (zikkaron)
column6: Exodus calls the Amalek event a zikkaron, orders it written in a book, and orders it recited to Joshua; this cognate-language use makes a remembered event both a page and an oral reminder.

column5: write a song, teach it, put it in mouths
column6: Moses is told to write the song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths, a concrete scriptural pattern for received words becoming communal recollection rather than remaining with the first recipient.

column5: scroll read daily so as to fear
column6: The king keeps the Torah scroll and reads it all his life to learn fear and obedience; it gives a close antecedent for the commentary's pages, recitation, retained word, and fearful hearer.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B009); Hebrew וזכרתם
column6: The tassel is to be seen so Israel will remember all the commandments and do them, showing a visible reminder that moves from memory into obedient action, as the commentary's reminder culminates in worship.

column5: ذ ك ر (B006/B007); Hebrew זכרי, divine name
column6: God calls the revealed name his zekheri, his memorial or renown through generations; this directly illuminates the commentary's two senses of dhikr as remembrance and honor attached to the divine name.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B009); ספר זכרון, fear, name
column6: A book of remembrance is written for those who fear the Lord and esteem his name, bringing together the commentary's written pages, fearful recipient, remembrance, and naming of God.

column5: trembling at God's word
column6: Isaiah identifies the one to whom God looks as the humble person who trembles at his word; this gives a precise biblical counterpart to the one who receives the reminder through khashyah.

column5: watchman hears then warns
column6: Ezekiel must hear a word from God and give warning to the people, the same two-stage relation the commentary draws between a messenger who receives speech and then reminds others.

column5: warning, refusal, watchman's deliverance
column6: When the warned wicked person does not turn, the person bears the consequence while the watchman has delivered himself; this closely parallels the commentary's claim that a reminder can benefit its giver even when its recipient forgets it.

column5: message heard but not beneficial without faith
column6: Hebrews explicitly says that a proclaimed message did not benefit its hearers because it was not joined with faith, a close Christian formulation of the commentary's unspoken recipient and conditional benefit.

column5: hear, hold fast, bear fruit
column6: The good soil hears the word, holds it fast in a good heart, and bears fruit; it concretely joins the commentary's container-like holding of a reminder to its beneficial result.

column5: heard teaching entrusted for further teaching
column6: What Timothy heard is to be entrusted to reliable people able to teach others, an explicit multi-step version of the commentary's move from received recitation to reminding a new audience.

column5: divine teacher will remind disciples
column6: The Paraclete will teach and remind the disciples of Jesus' words, placing divine preservation of a messenger's received speech beside his later task of reminder.

column5: gentle correction, hoped-for repentance
column6: The Lord's servant must correct opponents gently because God may grant repentance; it sharply parallels the commentary's gentle address to Pharaoh and its refusal to predict from the outside who will receive a reminder.

column5: one proclamation, life or death outcome
column6: The same apostolic aroma becomes death to some and life to others, a specific analogue to the commentary's one reminder that can benefit a reverent hearer yet be shunned by another.

column5: God gives growth, not the planter
column6: Paul distinguishes the speaker's planting and watering from God's giving growth; it clarifies the commentary's insistence that the reminder's unseen effect is not in the reminder-giver's control.

column5: saved if the proclaimed word is held fast
column6: The Corinthians are saved through the gospel if they hold fast the proclaimed word; this gives the commentary's conditional benefit a concrete link to retaining what was heard.

column5: guard the entrusted good deposit
column6: Timothy is commanded to guard the good deposit entrusted to him, closely matching the commentary's imagery of received speech being kept rather than lost before it is passed on.

column5: remember what was received and heard, then keep it
column6: The church is told to remember what it received and heard and to keep it; its sequence directly mirrors the commentary's recovery of a received word into active response.

column5: not a forgetful hearer, but a doer blessed
column6: James contrasts the forgetful hearer with one who perseveres in the law and acts, who is blessed in doing; this is a close counterpart to reminder, forgetting, and benefit.

column5: word dwelling within, mutual teaching, song
column6: When Christ's word dwells richly in believers they teach and admonish one another in song; it matches the commentary's account of an externally offered reminder becoming the listener's own worshipful speech.

column5: reminder and speech that gives no benefit
column6: Timothy is to remind believers, while warning that word-fighting is useful for nothing and ruins hearers; its explicit usefulness language closely frames the commentary's ن ف ع (B001) question about beneficial reminder.

column5: reader, hearers, and keepers of written prophecy
column6: The blessing falls on the reader, hearers, and keepers of a written prophecy, furnishing a Christian triad of page, public reading, internal reception, and benefit.

column5: liturgical action in remembrance
column6: Jesus commands a repeated meal to be done in remembrance of him; this provides a precise Christian instance of remembrance expressed as communal worship, relevant to the commentary's movement from dhikr to prayer.

column5: God opens a heart to attend to spoken message
column6: Lydia's heart is opened by the Lord so that she attends to Paul's speech, making visible in narrative form the commentary's claim that a reminder takes hold in a hidden interior place.

column5: proclaimer clear of hearers' blood after refusal
column6: After opposition to his proclamation, Paul says the hearers' blood is on their own heads and that he is clean; this is a Christian counterpart to the commentary's limited responsibility of the one who warns.

column5: speak whether they hear or refuse
column6: Ezekiel must speak God's words to rebels whether they hear or refuse, directly clarifying the commentary's distinction between the duty to remind and the hearer's uncoerced response.

column5: reprove a neighbor rather than share guilt
column6: Leviticus makes frank reproof an obligation toward a neighbor; this gives a Torah parallel to the commentary's account of warning as morally consequential also for the one who gives it.

column5: warning that may lead a nation to turn
column6: A nation warned of disaster may turn from evil and be spared; the verse supplies a prophetic logic for why a conditional reminder is still given before its benefit can be seen.

column5: tender heart on hearing the book, humbled fear
column6: Josiah's tender, humbled response when he hears the book of the law gives a narrative counterpart to the commentary's hearer whose inward fear makes remembrance fruitful.

column5: daily exhortation against hardened hearts
column6: Believers exhort one another daily so none is hardened by sin's deceit; it gives an ongoing communal form to the commentary's reminder that either reaches a hearer or is avoided.

column5: reminding people already established in truth
column6: The writer intends always to remind readers who already know and are established in the truth, closely supporting the commentary's point that tadhkirah retrieves what has been allowed to slip away rather than simply supplying novelty.

column5: received divine word actively at work in believers
column6: The Thessalonians receive the apostolic message as God's word, which works in believers; this supplies a Christian expression of the commentary's inward, not externally measurable, benefit of reminder.

column5: commandment is not too difficult
column6: Deuteronomy calls the commandment neither too difficult nor remote, a close scriptural counterpart to the commentary's divinely given ease that enables a word to be retained and acted upon.

column5: word near in mouth and heart for doing
column6: The word is very near, in mouth and heart so it can be done; this tightly connects the commentary's recitation, inner holding, and eventual practice.

column5: word stored in the heart against sin
column6: The psalmist stores God's word in the heart so as not to sin, a direct biblical image for the commentary's reminder becoming beneficial only when it is kept within.

column5: past deeds told to the coming generation
column6: The psalm refuses to hide God's praises, strength, and wonders from children but recounts them to a new generation, matching the commentary's reminder as retrieval of formerly given words and visible acts.

column5: remember God's works and keep commandments
column6: The next generation is to hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commandments; this links remembering, anti-forgetfulness, and practical response as the commentary does.

column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B009); Hebrew זכרון, ritual memorial
column6: Passover is called a zikkaron to be kept through generations; this cognate-language ritual instance illuminates the commentary's insistence that remembrance can be verbal and worshipful, not merely mental.

column5: water-crossing stones as a perpetual memorial
column6: The Jordan stones become a perpetual memorial after a passage through water, giving a close biblical analogue to the commentary's flood-water scene being made into a reminder for later hearers.

column5: ذ ك ر (B007); Hebrew זכרך, name and renown
column6: The psalm pairs God's enduring name with his zikhrekha through generations; it makes the commentary's secondary dhikr sense of honored renown concrete in a Hebrew cognate setting.

column5: prayers and alms as a memorial before God
column6: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, a Christian example of worshipful acts being designated remembrance, alongside the commentary's discussion of dhikr and prayer.

column5: Abraham commands household in the Lord's way
column6: God chooses Abraham so he will command his children and household to keep the Lord's way in righteousness and justice; this gives the named patriarch a biblical role as transmitter of prior instruction.

column5: Abraham keeps commands, statutes, and laws
column6: Alongside the commentary's "sheets of Abraham," Genesis portrays Abraham as keeping divine commands and laws but does not narrate an Abrahamic scroll; the contrast locates prior instruction in obedient practice rather than a named document.

column5: Christian reading of promise to Abraham
column6: Paul says Scripture announced good news beforehand to Abraham; this is a Christian interpretive extension of the commentary's claim that an earlier word belongs to Abraham, without identifying it with a literal Abrahamic sheet.

column5: righteous inherit land and dwell forever
column6: The psalm says the righteous inherit the land and dwell in it forever, the specific Zabur-like formulation that the commentary invokes when discussing an earlier written promise.

column5: meek inherit the earth
column6: Jesus' beatitude gives the meek the inheritance of the earth, a Christian revoicing of the land-inheritance formula that the commentary connects to the Psalms and earlier scripture.

column5: vision written plainly on tablets for readers
column6: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader; it is a direct biblical analogue for the commentary's concern that a revealed word be fixed on pages so it can pass beyond its first recipient.

column5: prophetic words written on a scroll
column6: Jeremiah is told to place all the spoken prophetic words on a scroll, providing a concrete parallel to the commentary's pairing of received speech, preservation, and a document for a community.

column5: written signs intended to bring faith and life
column6: John says selected signs are written so readers may believe and have life; this supplies a Christian written-text analogue to the commentary's question of when a reminder truly benefits its audience.

column5: creatures and earth teach about God's hand
column6: Job directs the hearer to animals, birds, earth, and fish as teachers of God's action; this closely parallels the commentary's claim that created order and pasture are already public material for reminder.

column5: God perceived through things made
column6: Romans says God's unseen power and divinity are perceived in created things, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's use of visible creation as a reminder of its maker.

column5: turn from vain things to the living creator
column6: Paul calls hearers away from vain things to the living God who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; it closely meets the commentary's Abrahamic contrast between powerless objects and the creating, guiding Lord.

column5: rain, fruitful seasons, food as divine witness
column6: God's rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness function as a witness in Paul's speech, directly complementing the commentary's creation-and-pasture material as a reminder offered in the world itself.

column5: idols do not profit
column6: Isaiah says the objects fashioned as idols do not profit; it is a precise Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic test of whether the objects of worship can give benefit or harm.

column5: idols can do neither harm nor good
column6: Jeremiah's idols cannot do evil or good and must be carried, directly matching the commentary's measure of worship by an object's incapacity to harm or benefit its devotee.

column5: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
column6: Proverbs says riches do not profit on the day of wrath while righteousness delivers; this supplies the commentary's final-day test of benefit against its contrast of wealth with a sound heart.

column5: worldly gain versus loss of life
column6: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life, a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's claim that material possessions fail the final measure of benefit.

column5: grass withers under the Lord's breath
column6: The grass withers and its flower fades when the Lord's breath blows; it closely echoes the commentary's pasture brought forth and then reduced to dark, dry refuse.

column5: withering grass contrasted with enduring divine word
column6: After grass and flower fade, God's word stands forever; the contrast gives a scriptural analogue to the commentary's opposition of what passes away to the reminder that remains and bears lasting fruit.

column5: rain waters earth and makes it sprout
column6: Rain and snow water the earth so that it sprouts and yields seed and bread, a specific meeting of the commentary's water, pasture, and useful growth imagery.

column5: word accomplishes its purpose and does not return empty
column6: God's word accomplishes its intended purpose rather than returning empty, an especially close counterpart to the commentary's question whether a reminder has actually proved beneficial.

column5: chaff and grain distinguish false and true word
column6: Jeremiah contrasts straw with grain while distinguishing dreams from God's word; this transforms the commentary's foam-and-residue image into a criterion for what remains as nourishing speech.

column5: wicked as chaff driven away
column6: The wicked are like chaff driven off by the wind, a close image for the commentary's foam or refuse that does not remain, set against what is enduring and fruitful.

column5: wheat gathered, chaff burned
column6: John's threshing image gathers wheat and destroys chaff, a Christian eschatological form of the commentary's distinction between what remains useful and what is cast away.

column5: flood sign that causes covenant remembrance
column6: The bow in the cloud makes God remember the everlasting covenant after the flood; it is a direct biblical instance of flood-water becoming an enduring reminder rather than a merely past event.

column5: Noah as herald of righteousness preserved through flood
column6: Second Peter calls Noah a herald of righteousness and joins his warning role to preservation through the flood, closely pairing the commentary's water-reminder image with the act of admonition.

column5: eight saved through water in the ark
column6: First Peter recalls a small company saved through water in Noah's ark, providing a Christian flood-and-vessel counterpart to the commentary's water scene in which people are carried for a later reminder.

column5: Moses' staff becomes a serpent
column6: Moses throws his ordinary staff down and it becomes a serpent, the same concrete transformation the commentary uses to show a practical staff becoming a divine sign.

column5: staff raised and hand stretched over the sea
column6: Both accounts associate Moses' staff with the sea, but Exodus specifies raising the staff and stretching out the hand to divide it, whereas the commentary recalls a striking action; the comparison preserves the narrated difference.

column5: staff strikes rock and brings water
column6: God directs Moses to strike the rock with the staff so water comes out, matching the commentary's use of the staff as an ordinary implement that becomes a sign-bearing means of water and provision.

column5: rod and staff as comfort
column6: The shepherd's rod and staff give comfort, supplying a biblical counterpart to the commentary's practical staff on which one leans and with which one guides animals.

column5: Moses' raised hands and inward direction to God
column6: The Mishnah says Moses' hands did not themselves make war; Israel prevailed when they directed their hearts upward. That interpretation makes the staff-associated sign depend on inward receptivity, as the commentary does.

column5: forgetting a word of Torah
column6: Avot treats forgetting even one learned word as spiritually grave while qualifying involuntary loss; this Jewish reading sharpens the commentary's contrast between a preserved teaching and an abandoned reminder.

column5: Abraham's destruction and exposure of idols
column6: Genesis Rabbah tells the idol-breaking episode in which Abraham exposes the idols' incapacity; it is a major Jewish interpretive parallel to the commentary's Abrahamic challenge about whether cult objects can hear, benefit, or harm.

column5: lost law rewritten so later people can find the path
column6: Ezra asks for inspired restoration of what was written in the burned law so people can find the path; it provides a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary's concern with a prior written word being recovered and retained.

column5: late calling after rejected reproof
column6: After rejecting wisdom's counsel, the hearers call but receive no answer; this gives a concrete biblical analogue to the commentary's late remembrance that no longer yields benefit.

column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B009); Hebrew זכור, Sabbath memory
column6: The Hebrew imperative zakhor, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر, makes remembering the Sabbath an act of sanctification; it gives a Torah precedent for remembrance becoming enacted worship.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B004); Hebrew זכרון, law in the mouth
column6: Passover is to be a sign and zikkaron so that the Lord's law will be in Israel's mouth, closely joining visible memorial, oral retention, and practice in the manner developed by the commentary.

column5: written tablets given for instruction
column6: God gives Moses tablets, law, and commandment written for Israel's instruction, a direct antecedent for the commentary's link between received revelation, written pages, and later teaching.

column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B009); Hebrew זכרון, trumpet memorial
column6: Trumpet blasts over offerings become a memorial before God; this is a precise ritual and auditory counterpart to the commentary's broad sense of dhikr as worshipful remembrance rather than bare recollection.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); remembering deliverance through Sabbath practice
column6: Israel is to remember slavery and redemption and therefore keep Sabbath; the verse makes memory of an earlier act the reason for present obedience, as the commentary makes recovered memory lead to prayer and action.

column5: words placed upon the heart
column6: The words commanded by God are to be upon the heart, furnishing an especially close Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's image of a reminder being held inwardly rather than merely heard.

column5: repeat the words to children in daily speech
column6: The heart-held words are to be repeated to children at home and on the way, an exact domestic form of the commentary's movement from retained revelation to another person's remembrance.

column5: warning not to forget the liberating Lord
column6: Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord after entering prosperity; it supplies the ethical danger against which the commentary defines reminder as the opposite of letting something escape the mind.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B001); remember God who gives power for wealth
column6: Israel must remember the Lord who gives power to acquire wealth, a cognate-root use that places remembrance beside material benefit and corrects self-sufficient possession in a way relevant to the commentary's test of what truly benefits.

column5: set hearts on the testimony and command children
column6: Moses tells Israel to set its heart on the testimony and command its children to do it, giving a close parallel to the commentary's sequence of inward retention, teaching, and ethical effect.

column5: word is life, not an empty matter
column6: The testimony is not an empty word but Israel's life and the source of long days; this directly supplies a biblical measure of the beneficial word that the commentary seeks in ن ف ع (B001).

column5: book in the mouth, meditation, doing, success
column6: Joshua keeps the Torah book in his mouth and meditates on it continually so as to do it and prosper, closely linking page, recitation, retained thought, action, and beneficial outcome.

column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B007); remembering God's name against worldly power
column6: Against reliance on chariots and horses, the psalmist remembers the name of the Lord; it illuminates the commentary's dhikr as both naming God and a counterweight to reliance on worldly means.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); wondrous works made memorable
column6: The Lord makes his wonders into a zekher, a memorial; this cognate-root formulation closely supports the commentary's claim that visible divine acts in the world are material for reminder.

column5: never forget precepts that give life
column6: The psalmist will not forget God's precepts because through them God gives life, directly binding anti-forgetfulness to benefit in the way the commentary's conditional reminder does.

column5: do not forget teaching; heart keeps commandments
column6: Proverbs pairs not forgetting instruction with the heart's keeping commandments, a compact wisdom analogue to the commentary's mental preservation of reminder before outward obedience.

column5: teaching written on the tablet of the heart
column6: Instruction is bound on the fingers and written on the tablet of the heart, joining physical inscription with interior retention and sharpening the commentary's pages-and-container imagery.

column5: words kept within and ready on the lips
column6: Wise words are pleasant when kept within and ready on the lips, a direct parallel to the commentary's claim that what is held mentally can become the hearer's own spoken word.

column5: message written on tablet and book for future days
column6: A prophetic charge is fixed on tablet and book for the time to come, offering a precise counterpart to the commentary's concern with preserving a word on pages for readers beyond its first hearing.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); remember and stand firm
column6: Isaiah calls transgressors to remember and stand firm; this cognate-root imperative supplies a Hebrew prophetic form of the commentary's tadhkirah addressed to those in danger of turning aside.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B006); remember former things and confess one God
column6: The command to remember former things leads to the confession that God alone is God, directly linking the commentary's prior-word remembrance with its insistence on the creator over powerless objects.

column5: look to Abraham as ancestral point of instruction
column6: Isaiah directs its hearers to look to Abraham and Sarah as the beginning of a blessed people; it gives a biblical way of making Abraham a remembered source for later communal instruction beside the commentary's Abrahamic sheets.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); fear, not remembering, and not laying to heart
column6: Isaiah asks whom Israel feared so that it neither remembered God nor laid him to heart, a striking inverse of the commentary's pairing of reverent fear with remembrance held inwardly.

column5: people forget God for days without number
column6: Jeremiah contrasts a bride who remembers clothing with a people that have forgotten God, providing a vivid prophetic parallel to the commentary's account of forgetfulness as abandonment of the very one to be remembered.

column5: Torah written within and on hearts
column6: Jeremiah relocates Torah from external writing to the inward heart; this complements and complicates the commentary's relation between earlier sheets and the listener's internal capacity to hold the reminder.

column5: righteous person warned, takes warning, and lives
column6: When the righteous person receives warning and does not sin, that person lives and the prophet is delivered; this necessary positive counterpart to the watchman scene maps the commentary's reminder when it actually benefits its hearer.

column5: hear prophetic speech but do not do it
column6: Ezekiel's audience listens to the prophet's pleasant song but refuses to do what it says; this gives a concrete biblical instance of hearing without the inward holding and action that the commentary calls beneficial.

column5: forgotten Torah followed by reciprocal forgetting
column6: Hosea says that because the people forgot God's Torah, God will forget their children; it makes the commentary's memory-forgetting contrast into a judicial outcome.

column5: priestly lips guard knowledge; people seek Torah from the mouth
column6: Knowledge is guarded by the priest's lips and sought by the people from that messenger's mouth, a close counterpart to the commentary's teacher who receives and explains a prior word to others.

column5: public Torah reading with explanation for understanding
column6: The Torah is read aloud, explained, and made understood; this exact public-reading scene supplies a Hebrew Bible analogue to the commentary's recitation followed by clarification for its listeners.

column5: study, do, and teach Torah
column6: Ezra sets his heart to study Torah, do it, and teach its statutes; this is a particularly clear threefold pattern for the commentary's received word, personal retention, and subsequent reminder.

column5: city believes warning and changes its practice
column6: Nineveh believes God's warning, fasts, and changes response; the scene shows the conditional benefit of a prophetic reminder becoming visible in a hearer's conduct.

column5: creation's visible goods should disclose their maker
column6: Wisdom faults people who see the good things of creation yet fail to know their maker, a Jewish-Hellenistic counterpart to the commentary's created order as a public reminder that can still be missed.

column5: human-made objects called gods
column6: Wisdom calls those unhappy who place hope in dead, human-made things named gods; it tightly parallels the commentary's Abrahamic examination of whether cult objects can truly help their worshippers.

column5: Moses receives Torah and transmits it through generations
column6: Avot's chain from Moses to Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly gives a Jewish traditional model for revelation preserved through successive human reminders.

column5: Moses' staff among twilight-created marvels
column6: By treating Moses' staff as one of the exceptional creations at twilight, Avot recasts the commentary's ordinary, useful staff as a primordial sign; the contrast is itself an instructive later reception of the object.

column5: remember ancestral deeds for honor and lasting name
column6: Mattathias tells his sons to remember the ancestors' deeds so as to receive honor and an everlasting name, directly connecting remembered prior tradition with the commentary's secondary sense of dhikr as renown.

column5: commandments of life and learned wisdom
column6: Baruch calls Israel to hear commandments of life and learn wisdom, a Jewish scriptural articulation of remembered instruction as life-giving benefit rather than mere information.

column5: pay attention to heard things lest they drift away
column6: Hebrews urges greater attention to what was heard so that it does not drift away, an exceptionally close New Testament formulation of the commentary's concern with a received word being lost unless held.

column5: hearer immediately forgets after looking
column6: James depicts the hearer who looks and then immediately forgets; this supplies the concrete negative image behind the commentary's contrast between reminder retained and reminder that passes by.

column5: let what was heard from the beginning abide
column6: The community is told to let the original message abide in it; this directly joins the commentary's prior word to an enduring inner dwelling rather than a momentary hearing.

column5: sayings treasured and pondered in the heart
column6: Mary keeps and ponders the sayings in her heart, a narrative counterpart to the commentary's image of an inward vessel that holds what has been spoken.

column5: hear God's word and keep it
column6: Jesus calls blessed those who hear God's word and keep it, a concise Christian parallel to the commentary's distinction between an offered reminder and beneficial, obedient retention.

column5: disciples remember a saying and believe Scripture
column6: After the resurrection the disciples remember Jesus' saying and believe both Scripture and his word, showing remembrance as a later recovery that makes prior speech intelligible.

column5: reading Scripture followed by explained proclamation
column6: Philip begins from the passage being read and explains its good news, closely matching the commentary's pattern of a received written word being made intelligible to another person.

column5: unceasing personal admonition to remember
column6: Paul tells the elders to remember his three years of unceasing warning; it gives a concrete apostolic example of reminder as sustained pastoral responsibility rather than coercive control.

column5: word of grace builds and gives inheritance
column6: Paul entrusts hearers to the word able to build them up and give an inheritance, an explicit account of a proclaimed word's beneficial result.

column5: former events written as instruction for later readers
column6: Israel's earlier events happened as examples and were written for instruction at the end of the ages, a close Christian parallel to the commentary's former pages and visible history functioning as reminder.

column5: former writings give instruction, endurance, and hope
column6: Paul says everything written beforehand was written for instruction so that readers may have hope, directly supporting the commentary's claim that previous scripture remains a usable word for later hearers.

column5: forgotten exhortation addressed to children
column6: Hebrews reproves readers for forgetting the exhortation that addresses them as children, making a prior scriptural warning itself the object that must be recalled.

column5: word choked by cares, riches, and pleasures
column6: In the thorny soil the heard word is choked by cares, riches, and pleasures and reaches no maturity; this directly supplies a Christian picture of why benefit may fail where the commentary contrasts lasting good with worldly preference.

column5: creation known but not honored or thanked
column6: Although people knew God, they neither honored nor thanked him and became futile in thought; this is the negative continuation of creation as a reminder that the commentary says can be seen yet not retained.

column5: deliberate overlooking of creation and water
column6: The opponents deliberately overlook the creation of earth through and by water through God's word, a striking Christian counterpart to the commentary's water-and-creation reminders that can be ignored.

column5: Noah warned of unseen things, reverent, building an ark
column6: Noah acts in reverent fear after a warning about unseen things and prepares an ark; it joins the commentary's fearful receiver, warning, and flood-water scene in one Christian retelling.

column5: heard words put into practice on rock
column6: The wise builder hears Jesus' words and does them, building on rock; this provides a vivid Christian counterpart to the commentary's demand that retained reminder issue in stable, beneficial action.

column5: Timothy sent to remind communities of apostolic ways
column6: Timothy is sent to remind the Corinthians of Paul's ways as taught everywhere, an unusually exact New Testament instance of a messenger being delegated to perform remembrance for others.

column5: learned, received, heard, seen, then practiced
column6: The Philippians are to practice what they learned, received, heard, and saw; its ordered reception-to-practice sequence closely reflects the commentary's account of reminder becoming the hearer's own deed.

column5: sacred writings able to make wise for salvation
column6: Sacred writings are able to make Timothy wise for salvation, a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's prior sheets as a word whose benefit lies in the good to which it leads.

column5: annual sacrificial remembrance of sins
column6: The sacrifices contain an annual remembrance of sins, a distinct Christian liturgical use of memory that bears on the commentary's discussion of dhikr's ritual as well as mental forms.

column5: honor with lips while heart remains distant
column6: Jesus contrasts lip-honor with a heart far from God; this sharpens the commentary's warning that spoken remembrance is only a later branch if the inward holding of the word is absent.

column5: land drinks rain and yields crop, receiving blessing
column6: Land that drinks repeated rain and bears a useful crop receives blessing; it gives a Christian agrarian analogue to the commentary's water, pasture, and beneficial remainder imagery.

column5: thorns after rain are rejected and burned
column6: Land yielding thorns after the same rain is rejected and ends in burning, a specific contrary image for the commentary's one reminder producing different outcomes in its hearers.

column5: remember the one who speaks God's word and honor that speaker
column6: The Didache tells its hearer to remember day and night the person who speaks God's word and to honor that person; it is an early Christian reception of the teacher-reminder relation developed in the commentary.
